analysis.one_liner: Strips the National Labor Relations Board of its power to prosecute employers and issue workplace rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have stripped the labor board of its power to prosecute unfair labor practices, was referred to a House subcommittee in April 2013 and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the National Labor Relations Act so the NLRB could investigate unfair labor practices but not prevent them. It would repeal the Board's power to issue and prosecute complaints, limit its rulemaking to purely internal matters, and instead let aggrieved parties sue directly in federal court. Practically, the government would stop enforcing labor law against employers who fire, retaliate against, or interfere with workers, and workers would have to pay for their own lawsuits instead.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers accused of unfair labor practices would be the main beneficiaries. The NLRB would no longer prosecute complaints against them, and it could no longer write rules affecting their substantive rights. Workers would gain only the theoretical ability to sue employers directly in federal court, at their own expense.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the General Counsel's authority to issue and prosecute unfair labor practice complaints before the Board, ending the agency's enforcement role [S2][S3].
It limits Board rulemaking to internal functions and prohibits any rule affecting the substantive rights of employers, employees, or unions [S2][S3].
It replaces Board prosecution with a private right of action: an aggrieved party could sue in federal court for relief including injunctions [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers who rely on the NLRB would bear the cost. The Board would no longer investigate and prosecute employers on their behalf, so a worker facing retaliation or an illegal firing would have to bring and finance a federal lawsuit alone.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have stripped the NLRB of its power to prevent unfair labor practices and to issue and prosecute complaints, leaving enforcement to private lawsuits that individual workers would have to fund themselves [S2][S3].
It would have barred the Board from issuing any rules affecting the substantive rights of workers, employers, or unions, sharply limiting the agency's ability to adapt workplace law [S2][S3].

A good-faith objection from supporters: the NLRB's General Counsel both investigates and prosecutes complaints, and the Board's rulemaking has sometimes changed substantive rights without congressional action; the bill would have moved enforcement into ordinary federal courts instead [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's backers could argue that the NLRB's General Counsel has too much unchecked power to prosecute employers and that the Board's rulemaking has gone beyond what Congress intended, so forcing disputes into regular federal courts would add due process. But the costs fall heavily on workers: the NLRB currently investigates and prosecutes unfair labor practices at no cost to the employee; a private civil action model would leave individual workers to fund their own federal litigation and seek injunctions, which is far more expensive and slower. On balance, the bill would have made labor-law enforcement substantially weaker for workers while removing a meaningful check on employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House education committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 15, 2013 and referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day [S5].
On April 23, 2013 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, where it stayed for the rest of the 113th Congress [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2015 with no further action recorded on the bill [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers facing union complaints are better off that it died only in the sense that the status quo held; the NLRB's existing enforcement and rulemaking authority remained intact because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; NLRB kept its authority

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to the Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions, and took no further action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 56 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support recorded, though the bill never advanced far enough to produce a floor vote.

industries.industry: Employers facing union organizing and labor complaints
industries.note: The bill would have ended NLRB prosecution of unfair labor practices and barred the Board from substantive rulemaking, removing the main enforcement mechanism against employers accused of firing or retaliating against workers. Workers would instead have to bring and fund their own federal lawsuits.

Unions rely on the NLRB to prosecute employer unfair labor practices and on Board rulemaking to update workplace law. Losing both would have left unions with private litigation as the only remedy, a far slower and costlier route.
